html_en:
The AI model race is accelerating faster than anyone expected — and the economic ripple effects are only beginning to be understood.

GPT-5.6 Sol Arrives, and the Benchmarks Aren't the Point

OpenAI's latest release, GPT-5.6 Sol, is generating serious buzz — and not just from the usual benchmark-watchers. Sam Altman offered perhaps the most memorable (if tongue-in-cheek) quality signal:

"There are a lot of benchmarks that suggest 5.6 Sol is the best model in the world right now, but the most reliable way to tell is that Elon is obsessed with me again." — @sama

Beyond the trolling, the practical reception from builders has been warm. @thsottiaux — who has been vocal about prior model limitations — made a point of cataloguing the improvements in his announcement thread:

"At different times you complained about speed, code slop, frontend quality... GPT 5.6 Sol is: fast and token efficient, hardcore at back-end dev, great at front-end, does not use useEffect everywhere." — @thsottiaux

That last point — the dreaded useEffect antipattern — may seem like a minor gripe, but it reflects something real: AI coding models have historically produced syntactically valid but architecturally sloppy code, and developers notice. @zarazhangrui echoed the sentiment on frontend quality with a simple "5.6 Sol is very good at front end 👌"

The Jailbreak That Wasn't: Running Sol Through Claude's Shell

The most technically creative response to the new release came from @thsottiaux, who published a clever workaround for those not yet ready to switch apps — routing GPT-5.6 Sol through Claude Code's interface via a proxy alias he dubbed claudex:

"If you aren't yet bold enough to install the Codex app, you can stay in the presence of your orange crab and point it at GPT 5.6 Sol. Takes 5 minutes."

alias claudex='CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL=gpt-5.6-sol \ CLAUDE_CODE_ALWAYS_ENABLE_EFFORT=1 \ ...' — @thsottiaux

It's a small but telling moment: developers are increasingly treating model providers as interchangeable inference backends, with the interface layer — Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf — becoming the stickier product. The model wars may be heating up, but the UX wars are the ones that determine daily habits.

Jevons Is Having His Moment

The deeper conversation happening in parallel is about what all this capability actually does to labor markets. @swyx made the case for thinking about it through the lens of Jevons Paradox — the 19th-century economic observation that efficiency improvements in resource use tend to increase total consumption, not reduce it:

"As the efficiency of labor goes up / unit cost of knowledge work goes broadly down, the demand for total work and better knowledge goes up, not down. What happened to coding isn't the exception; it's the herald." — @swyx

Aaron Levie made a similar argument, grounding it in observable data rather than economic theory:

"The job that AI was supposed to replace is experiencing the opposite of the expected outcome. Software job postings are outpacing other fields. Because software now is much lower cost per unit, people want way more of it. So we start to use software for all new things and people and companies light up more software projects than ever before... Agents will cause more abundance than replacement." — @levie

Both are making the same bet: that AI-driven cost reduction in knowledge work is more likely to resemble the industrial revolution's effect on manufacturing — massive expansion of total output and employment — than the ATM's effect on bank tellers (a partial, localized replacement). It's an optimistic read, and not everyone shares it. But the early data from software hiring is at least consistent with it.

The Booking.com CEO on Why Moats Don't Exist

On this week's No Priors podcast, hosts sat down with Glenn Fogel, the 27-year veteran CEO of Booking Holdings — the $100B+ travel giant that started as a scrappy Priceline. The conversation ranged across AI strategy and competitive dynamics, with Fogel offering a refreshingly unsentimental take on defensibility: Watch/Listen: Travel Through the Lens of AI with Booking.com CEO Glenn Fogel — No Priors

"There is no such thing as a moat. There is no such thing as somewhere you're gonna be protected against innovation. Today, we have a competitive advantage on areas. Absolutely. But those can go away tomorrow. The only way to win long term is to continue to develop new services, new ways to do things." — Glenn Fogel

For a company sitting on decades of booking data, supplier relationships, and brand recognition across Booking.com, Kayak, Priceline, and OpenTable, that's a notably humble posture. Fogel's career arc — IBM mainframe operator, Wall Street banker, failed novelist, accidental travel tech legend — gives him a particular credibility when he warns would-be disruptors to understand the complexity of the business before "committing their capital." The AI era is generating no shortage of travel startup pitches. His implicit message: the incumbents are not asleep.

That's the digest for today. The throughline: cheaper intelligence creates more demand for intelligence, not less — and the companies and individuals who internalize that fastest will be the ones setting the pace.
html_zh:
GPT-5.6 Sol 的横空出世与知识经济的"杰文斯悖论"成为今日科技圈的核心议题——效率提升，需求反而激增，这一古老的经济规律正在以全新面貌重演。

🚀 GPT-5.6 Sol：新王登基，战场重划

OpenAI 最新旗舰模型 GPT-5.6 Sol 正在成为开发者社区的热议焦点。来自社区的反馈显示，这款模型在前端开发、后端逻辑和响应速度上均有显著提升。

@thsottiaux 直接点名了过去用户的痛点，并宣告这些问题已成历史：

"在不同时期你们抱怨过速度慢、代码质量差、前端效果糟糕……每次发布我们都有改进，GPT-5.6 Sol 现在做到了：快速且 token 高效、后端硬核、前端出色、不再到处乱用 useEffect。"
— @thsottiaux

更有趣的是，他还分享了一个"野路子"技巧——通过 CLIProxyAPI 将 GPT-5.6 Sol 接入 Claude Code，并取名"claudex"，让两大生态的用户都能无缝体验新模型。这条推文获得近 4000 点赞，足见开发者社区的热情。

社区评测也印证了这一判断。@zarazhangrui 简洁地给出结论："5.6 Sol 在前端上表现非常好 👌"

而 Sam Altman 则用一贯的幽默方式为新模型背书：

"有很多基准测试表明 5.6 Sol 是目前世界上最好的模型，但最可靠的判断方式是——Elon 又开始疯狂盯着我了。"
— @sama

📈 杰文斯悖论降临知识工作：效率越高，需求越旺

当 AI 编程工具让软件开发成本大幅下降时，软件工程师的岗位需求非但没有萎缩，反而在加速增长。这一现象正在引发科技界对"替代论"的深刻反思。

Aaron Levie 用通俗语言解释了这背后的经济逻辑：

"软件现在每单位成本大幅下降，人们就想要更多的软件。于是我们开始把软件用于所有新事物，公司和个人启动的软件项目比以往任何时候都多。但因为这份工作并没有被完全自动化（而且在可预见的未来也不会），你仍然需要理解这些系统的人来维护代码、决定构建什么、长期运营它、更新它……这一切都需要人来完成。智能体带来的是更多的丰裕，而不是替代。"
— @levie

@swyx 则从更宏观的视角补充了这一论点，指出"杰文斯悖论"的影响远未被充分内化：

"随着劳动效率提升、知识工作单位成本全面下降，总体工作需求和对更好知识的需求反而上升，而非下降。编程领域发生的事不是例外；它是先兆。"
— @swyx

简言之：AI 工具不是在消灭工程师，而是在扩大整个软件市场的蛋糕。

🏨 传统巨头的 AI 生存哲学：Booking.com CEO 的战壕智慧

在 No Priors 播客的最新一期中，Booking Holdings CEO Glenn Fogel 分享了他对 AI 时代竞争壁垒的独到见解。Watch/Listen: Travel Through the Lens of AI with Booking.com CEO Glenn Fogel

这位在公司深耕 27 年、亲历市值从数亿美元暴涨至 1800 亿美元的老将，对"护城河"的执念给出了近乎颠覆性的回答：

"护城河根本不存在。没有任何地方能让你免受创新冲击。今天我们在某些领域拥有竞争优势，这是绝对的。但明天这些优势就可能消失。长期取胜的唯一方法，是持续开发新服务、新的做事方式。"
— Glenn Fogel，No Priors

对于那些试图用 AI 颠覆旅行行业的新进入者，Fogel 也毫不客气地泼了冷水："如果你觉得可以轻松进来、干掉这些大玩家，我建议你在决定投入资本之前，先真正搞懂这门生意。"

这番话对当下蜂拥入场 AI 垂直应用的创业者而言，或许是最值得玩味的提醒。

⚽ 花絮：科技圈的世界杯深夜

今晚，阿根廷队的世界杯赛事意外成为科技推特的共同背景音。Matt Turck、Peter Yang、Nikunj 等投资人和创业者纷纷实时发推，吐槽阿根廷对阵世界排名 19 位球队时的惊险表现。Guillermo Rauch 则只留下意味深长的三个字："Easy money（瑞士法郎）"——暗示他可能在某支球队上押对了注。

比 AI 基准测试更难预测的，永远是足球。
